Radzymin Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Radzymin, Poland

Demolished. Jews are recorded in Radzymin from the late 18th century, and the town later became seat of the Radzymin Hasidic dynasty; by 1921, 2,209 Jews made up 55% of the population, most murdered at Treblinka in 1942. The cemetery is first documented in an 1775 diocesan inspection record. Jews who died during the 1794 Kościuszko Uprising were buried here, and in 1903 Rabbi Szlomo Jehoszua Dawid Guterman, son of the dynasty's founder, was interred at the site. During the Holocaust, victims of the Radzymin Ghetto - including a typhus epidemic - were buried here, and Germans continued executions on the grounds until at least autumn 1943. Poland formally closed the cemetery in 1964, and a park was built on the site around 1970. In the 1980s-90s, Radzymin Jews living in Israel and France funded a sarcophagus-style monument at Rabbi Guterman's grave, later expanded into a full ohel in 2015-2016 through a joint effort by Krzysztof Bielawski, Joseph Deutsch, and Igor Basaj. In 2017, tombstones uncovered during a supermarket's construction on a former dairy site were returned to the cemetery.
